facts.statement: The genus Mosasaurus was named by William Daniel Conybeare in 1822.
facts.quote: authority: Conybeare, 1822

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Mosasaurus is Mosasaurus hoffmanni.
facts.quote: type_species: Mosasaurus hoffmanni

facts.statement: Species described within the genus Mosasaurus include M. missouriensis, M. conodon, M. lemonnieri, and M. beaugei.
facts.quote: subdivision: *M. missouriensis (Harlan, 1834) M. conodon (Cope, 1881) M. lemonnieri (Dollo, 1889) M. beaugei Arambourg, 1952

facts.statement: The first fossils of Mosasaurus were discovered as skulls in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in the late 18th century.
facts.quote: the first fossils of Mosasaurus were found as skulls in a chalk quarry near the Dutch city of Maastricht in the late 18th century

facts.statement: A skull discovered in 1778 was nicknamed the "great animal of Maastricht".
facts.quote: One skull discovered in 1778 was famously nicknamed the "great animal of Maastricht".

facts.statement: The first known Mosasaurus fossil, cataloged as TM 7424, is currently displayed at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.
facts.quote: This specimen, cataloged as TM 7424, is now on display at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.

facts.statement: A second skull was found in the same quarry in 1778, which attracted the attention of Johann Leonard Hoffmann.
facts.quote: Later, in 1778, the quarry produced a second skull that caught the attention of Johann Leonard Hoffmann

facts.statement: After being seized during the French Revolutionary Wars, the second skull was sent to the National Museum of Natural History in France in 1795 and numbered MNHN AC 9648.
facts.quote: After its seizure, the specimen was sent to the National Museum of Natural History, France in 1795 and later numbered as MNHN AC 9648.

facts.statement: William Daniel Conybeare coined the genus name Mosasaurus in a 1822 book by James Parkinson.
facts.quote: In a 1822 book by James Parkinson, William Daniel Conybeare coined the genus Mosasaurus

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell added the specific epithet hoffmanni to the species name in 1829 to honor Johann Leonard Hoffmann.
facts.quote: In 1829, Gideon Mantell added the specific epithet hoffmanni, in honor to Hoffmann.

facts.statement: The largest species, Mosasaurus hoffmanni, is estimated to reach a maximum length of 12 meters.
facts.quote: The largest species, M. hoffmanni, is estimated to measure up to 12 m in maximum length.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had four limbs shaped into paddles used for steering underwater.
facts.quote: Its four limbs were shaped into paddles to steer the animal underwater.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus fossils have been found in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and Antarctica.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus fossils have been found in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and Antarctica.

facts.statement: Scientists continue to debate whether the closest living relatives of Mosasaurus are monitor lizards or snakes.
facts.quote: The exact affinities of Mosasaurus as a squamate remain controversial, and scientists continue to debate whether its closest living relatives are monitor lizards or snakes.

facts.statement: An unclear diagnosis of the type species M. hoffmanni led to historically problematic classification issues.
facts.quote: an unclear diagnosis (description of distinguishing features) of the type species M. hoffmanni led to a historically problematic classification.

facts.statement: A fossil skeleton identified as a 49-foot-long fish was discovered by the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1804 near the Missouri River.
facts.quote: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition discovered a now-lost fossil skeleton alongside the Missouri River, which was identified as a 49 ft long fish.

facts.statement: In 1818, a fossil from Monmouth County, New Jersey became the first North American specimen correctly identified as a Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1818, a fossil from Monmouth County, New Jersey became the first North American specimen to be correctly recognized as a Mosasaurus by scientists of the time.

facts.statement: Georg August Goldfuss published a study on the M. missouriensis fossil material in 1845.
facts.quote: Georg August Goldfuss in Bonn for research, who published a study in 1845.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy established the combination M. missouriensis in 1857 following a suggestion by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer.
facts.quote: Joseph Leidy erected the new combination M. missouriensis after this suggestion in 1857, which has since entered common use.

facts.statement: The missing snout of the M. missouriensis type specimen was found in 2004 in the MNHN collections under catalog number MNHN 9587.
facts.quote: The snout was finally found in 2004 in the collections of the MNHN under the catalog number MNHN 9587, thus confirming the initial suspicion expressed by von Meyer and followed by other authors.

facts.statement: Louis Dollo first described M. lemonnieri in 1889 based on a specimen with a relatively complete skull and cervical vertebrae found in a quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.
facts.quote: M. lemonnieri was first described in 1889 by Louis Dollo based on a specimen comprising a relatively complete skull and several cervical (neck) vertebrae, discovered in a quarry owned by the Solvay S.A. company in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of M. lemonnieri, cataloged as IRSNB R28, was donated by Alfred Lemonnier, after whom the species was named.
facts.quote: This specimen, since numbered as IRSNB R28, is one of the many fossils donated by the then director of the company, Alfred Lemonnier, Dollo naming the species in his honor.

facts.statement: Camille Arambourg named M. beaugei in 1952 as part of a research program on Moroccan phosphate deposits that began in 1934.
facts.quote: M. beaugei was named in 1952 by Camille Arambourg as part of a large-scale research program on the phosphate deposits of Morocco that had been ongoing since 1934.

facts.statement: M. beaugei was initially described from nine isolated teeth found in the Oulad Abdoun and Ganntour phosphate basins and dedicated to Alfred Beaugé.
facts.quote: The species was initially described from nine isolated teeth discovered in the phosphate basins of Oulad Abdoun and Ganntour, and was dedicated to Alfred Beaugé, then director-general of the OCP Group, who supported Arambourg's research.

facts.statement: In 2004, Nathalie Bardet and colleagues reexamined the original material of M. beaugei and described additional fossils, including two well-preserved skulls from the Oulad Abdoun Basin.
facts.quote: In 2004, Nathalie Bardet and colleagues reexamined Arambourg's original material and concluded that only three of these teeth could be confidently referred to M. beaugei, while also describing additional fossils of the species, including two relatively well-preserved skulls recovered from the Oulad Abdoun Basin.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel demonstrated in 1854 that Mosasaurus possessed fully aquatic flippers rather than limbs for walking.
facts.quote: In 1854, Hermann Schlegel proved how Mosasaurus actually had fully aquatic flippers.

facts.statement: The flippers of Mosasaurus are broad, flat, and shaped like paddles.
facts.quote: They are also broad, flat, and form a paddle.

facts.statement: Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins created a life-size concrete sculpture of Mosasaurus between 1852 and 1854 for the Crystal Palace Park in London.
facts.quote: One of the earliest depictions of Mosasaurus in paleoart is a life-size concrete sculpture created by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins between 1852 and 1854 as part of the collection of sculptures of prehistoric animals on display at the Crystal Palace Park in London.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus was a derived mosasaur characterized by advanced evolutionary traits including a fully aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus was a type of derived mosasaur, or a latecoming member with advanced evolutionary traits such as a fully aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had a streamlined body, an elongated tail with a downturned two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.
facts.quote: As such, it had a streamlined body, an elongated tail ending with a downturn supporting a two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.

facts.statement: The taxonomic validity of M. lemonnieri has been the subject of long-standing debate.
facts.quote: The taxonomic validity of M. lemonnieri was long debated.

facts.statement: In 2004, Mulder, Cornelissen, and Verding suggested that M. lemonnieri might be a juvenile form of M. hoffmanni, a hypothesis contested by later anatomical studies.
facts.quote: In 2004, Eric Mulder, Dirk Cornelissen, and Louis Verding suggested M. lemonnieri could be a juvenile form of M. hoffmanni based on the argument that significant differences could be explained by age-based variation.

facts.statement: Subsequent research contested the idea that M. lemonnieri is a juvenile of M. hoffmanni by highlighting major anatomical differences, especially in dentition.
facts.quote: However, this was contested by subsequent work that highlighted major anatomical distinctions between the two species, primarily in the dentition.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel demonstrated that Mosasaurus phalanges lacked muscle or tendon attachments, making walking impossible.
facts.quote: He clarified that earlier interpretations of claws were erroneous and demonstrated how the phalanges show no indication of muscle or tendon attachment, which would make walking impossible.

facts.statement: Derived mosasaurs like Mosasaurus are now understood to have builds similar to ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales due to convergent evolution.
facts.quote: While in the past derived mosasaurs were depicted as akin to giant flippered sea snakes, it is now understood that they were more similar in build to other large marine vertebrates such as ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales through convergent evolution.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus hoffmanni is considered one of the largest known marine reptiles.
facts.quote: The type species, M. hoffmanni, is one of the largest marine reptiles known

facts.statement: Russell (1967) proposed that the jaw length of M. hoffmanni equals one-tenth of its total body length.
facts.quote: Russell (1967) wrote that the length of the jaw equalled one tenth of the body length in the species

facts.statement: Grigoriev (2014) estimated the maximum length of M. hoffmanni to be 17.1 meters based on a lower jaw measuring 171 cm.
facts.quote: Grigoriev (2014) used the largest lower jaw attributed to M. hoffmanni (CCMGE 10/2469, also known as the Penza specimen; measuring 171 cm in length) to estimate a maximum length of 17.1 m

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar (1995) estimated a maximum length of 17.6 meters for M. hoffmanni using a jaw-to-body ratio.
facts.quote: Lingham-Soliar (1995) estimated a larger maximum length of 17.6 m via the same ratio

facts.statement: The 1:10 jaw-to-body ratio from Russell (1967) lacks explicit justification and is considered likely overestimated by Cleary et al. (2018).
facts.quote: No explicit justification for the 1:10 ratio was provided in Russell (1967), and it has been considered to be probably overestimated by Cleary et al. (2018)

facts.statement: Federico Fanti and colleagues (2014) argued that M. hoffmanni length is likely closer to seven times the skull length rather than ten.
facts.quote: In 2014, Federico Fanti and colleagues alternatively argued that the total length of M. hoffmanni was more likely closer to seven times the length of the skull

facts.statement: Everhart and colleagues (2016) suggested a quadrate bone 150% larger than average could indicate an M. hoffmanni individual around 18 meters long.
facts.quote: One such bone is a quadrate (NHMM 003892) which is 150% larger than the average size, which Everhart and colleagues in 2016 reported can be extrapolated to scale an individual around 18 m in length

facts.statement: Dollo estimated that M. lemonnieri grew to a length of 7 to 10 meters.
facts.quote: Dollo estimated M. lemonnieri grew to around 7 to 10 m in length

facts.statement: Dollo recorded that the skull of M. lemonnieri constituted approximately one-eleventh of the whole body.
facts.quote: He also measured the dimensions of IRSNB R 29 and recorded that the skull constituted approximately one-eleventh of the whole body

facts.statement: Bardet et al. (2015) estimated M. beaugei grew to 8 to 10 meters in length with skulls typically around 1 meter.
facts.quote: Bardet et al. (2015) estimated that M. beaugei grew to a total length of 8-10 m, their skulls typically measuring around 1 m in length

facts.statement: The Mosasaurus skull is conical and tapers to a short snout extending slightly beyond the frontmost teeth.
facts.quote: The skull of Mosasaurus is conical and tapers off to a short snout which extends a little beyond the frontmost teeth

facts.statement: The snout of M. hoffmanni is blunt, whereas the snout of M. lemonnieri is pointed.
facts.quote: In M. hoffmanni, this snout is blunt, while in M. lemonnieri it is pointed

facts.statement: A single row of foramina above the gum line in Mosasaurus jaws holds the terminal branches of jaw nerves.
facts.quote: Above the gum line in both jaws, a single row of small pits known as foramina are lined parallel to the jawline; they are used to hold the terminal branches of jaw nerves

facts.statement: In M. hoffmanni, the external nares measure around 21% to 24% of the skull's length.
facts.quote: The external nares (nostril openings) are moderately sized and measure around 21–24% of the skull's length in M. hoffmanni

facts.statement: The nares in M. hoffmanni are placed further back than in nearly all other mosasaurs, beginning above the fourth or fifth maxillary teeth.
facts.quote: They are placed further toward the back of the skull than in nearly all other mosasaurs (exceeded only by Goronyosaurus), and begin above the fourth or fifth maxillary teeth

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were specialized for cutting prey and featured highly prismatic enamel surfaces with two opposite cutting edges.
facts.quote: The features of teeth in Mosasaurus vary across species, but unifying characteristics include a design specialized for cutting prey, highly prismatic surfaces (enamel circumference shaped by flat sides called prisms), and two opposite cutting edges.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were generally large and robust, except in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri which had more slender teeth.
facts.quote: Mosasaurus teeth are large and robust except for those in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri, which instead have more slender teeth.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of M. hoffmanni and M. missouriensis were finely serrated, whereas M. conodon and M. lemonnieri lacked serrations.
facts.quote: The cutting edges in M. hoffmanni and M. missouriensis are finely serrated, while in M. conodon and M. lemonnieri serrations do not exist.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of M. beaugei possessed minute wrinkles called crenulations rather than being serrated or smooth.
facts.quote: The cutting edges of M. beaugei are neither serrated nor smooth, but instead possess minute wrinkles known as crenulations.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were thecodont, meaning their roots were deeply cemented within the jaw bone.
facts.quote: The dentition was thecodont (tooth roots deeply cemented within the jaw bone).

facts.statement: Mosasaurus teeth were constantly replaced as new teeth developed within the roots of old ones and pushed them out.
facts.quote: Teeth were constantly shed through a process where the replacement tooth developed within the root of the original tooth and then pushed it out of the jaw.

facts.statement: Studies measured the rate of odontoblast deposition in M. hoffmanni teeth at an average of 10.9 micrometers per day.
facts.quote: Chemical studies conducted on a M. hoffmanni maxillary tooth measured an average rate of deposition of odontoblasts, the cells responsible for the formation of dentin, at 10.9 um per day.

facts.statement: All Mosasaurus species possessed seven cervical vertebrae, though counts for other vertebrae varied among species.
facts.quote: All species of Mosasaurus have seven cervical vertebrae, but other vertebral counts vary among them.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus had an unusually deep rib cage forming a semicircle, resulting in a barrel-shaped chest compared to other mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Compared to other mosasaurs, the rib cage of Mosasaurus is unusually deep and forms an almost perfect semicircle, giving it a barrel-shaped chest.

facts.statement: Extensive cartilage likely connected the ribs to the sternum in Mosasaurus, facilitating breathing and compression in deep water.
facts.quote: Rather than being fused together, extensive cartilage likely connected the ribs with the sternum, which would have facilitated breathing movements and compression when in deeper waters.

facts.statement: The bone texture of Mosasaurus was virtually identical to modern whales, indicating high aquatic adaptation and neutral buoyancy.
facts.quote: The texture of the bones is virtually identical with in modern whales, which indicates Mosasaurus possessed a high range of aquatic adaptation and neutral buoyancy as seen in cetaceans.

facts.statement: Skeletal features support the existence of a large, powerful paddle-like fluke in Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: These and other features support a large and powerful paddle-like fluke in Mosasaurus.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus forelimbs were wide and robust, with fan-shaped scapulae and humeri that were wider than tall.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Mosasaurus are wide and robust. The scapula and humerus are fan-shaped and wider than tall.

facts.statement: The ilium in Mosasaurus was rod-like and slender, being around 1.5 times longer than the femur in M. missouriensis.
facts.quote: The ilium is rod-like and slender; in M. missouriensis, it is around 1.5 times longer than the femur.

facts.statement: The Mosasaurus femur was about twice as long as it was wide, with articular facets meeting at an angle of approximately 120 degrees.
facts.quote: The femur itself is about twice as long as it is wide and ends at the distal side in a pair of distinct articular facets (of which one connects to the ilium and the other to the paddle bones) that meet at an angle of approximately 120°.

facts.statement: The Mosasaurus hindlimb paddles were supported by four sets of digits.
facts.quote: In the hindlimbs, the paddle is supported by four sets of digits.

facts.statement: Mosasaurus is the type genus of the family Mosasauridae and subfamily Mosasaurinae, and belongs to the order Squamata.
facts.quote: As the type genus of the family Mosasauridae and the subfamily Mosasaurinae, Mosasaurus is a member of the order Squamata (which comprises lizards and snakes).

facts.statement: 19th-century scientists failed to provide a proper diagnosis for Mosasaurus due to undefined nomenclatural rules, leading to ambiguity in the genus definition.
facts.quote: Because nomenclatural rules were not well-defined at the time, 19th century scientists did not give Mosasaurus a proper diagnosis during its initial descriptions, which led to ambiguity in how the genus is defined.

facts.statement: In a 2026 revision, Sharpe and colleagues consider M. conodon a nomen dubium because its holotype is too fragmentary to be diagnostic.
facts.quote: In their 2026 revision of M. lemonnieri, Sharpe and colleagues consider M. conodon as a nomen dubium, deeming its holotype too fragmentary to be diagnostic.
